title: Change of Basis and Similarity

intro.x: A vector is a geometric object; its coordinates are a description of it relative to a chosen basis. Change the basis and the same vector gets different coordinates, and the same linear map gets a different matrix. This chapter works out exactly how. The central idea of the rest of the book follows: choose the basis so that the matrix of a map is as simple as possible (diagonal, if we can). Matrices that represent the same map in different bases are called similar, and the properties that all similar matrices share, such as determinant, trace and eigenvalues, are the true invariants of the map.

blocks.x: Let $\mathcal{B}=(\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_n)$ and $\mathcal{C}=(\mathbf{c}_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}_n)$ be two bases of the same space $V$. A vector $\mathbf{v}$ has coordinates $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}$. How are they related?

The change-of-basis matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is $P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}=[\id]_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$, the matrix whose $j$-th column is $[\mathbf{b}_j]_{\mathcal{C}}$, the coordinates of the old basis vectors in the new basis.
For every $\mathbf{v}\in V$,
[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}=P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}.
The matrix $P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$ is invertible and $P_{\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathcal{C}}=P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}^{-1}$.
This is Theorem 9.7 for $T=\id$. The identity map is invertible, so by Theorem 9.16 its matrix is invertible with the stated inverse.
Let $\mathcal{S}=(\mathbf{e}_1,\mathbf{e}_2)$ be the standard basis and $\mathcal{B}=((1,1),(1,-1))$. The matrix whose columns are the $\mathcal{B}$-vectors written in standard coordinates is
P_{\mathcal{S}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
Hence $\mathbf{v}=(5,1)$ has $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}=P_{\mathcal{S}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}^{-1}(5,1)\T=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}(5,1)\T=(3,2)\T$, as found by hand in Chapter 7.

blocks.caption: Two coordinate systems for the same plane: the grid of the standard basis and the skew axes of $\mathcal{B}=(\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2)$. The vector $\mathbf{v}=(2,0)$ is one object with two descriptions: $(2,0)$ in the standard basis and $(1,1)$ in $\mathcal{B}$.

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: which direction does the matrix go?

blocks.x: The columns of $P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$ express the old basis in terms of the new one, and the matrix converts old coordinates to new coordinates. When the new basis is the standard one, $P_{\mathcal{S}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$ is simply the matrix with the basis vectors as columns, and converting to the nonstandard basis requires its inverse. Mixing these up is the most common error in this chapter; a good habit is to read the subscripts as arrows, “$\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}$ takes $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates in, gives $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates out”.

sections.title: Changing the matrix of a map

blocks.x: Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear operator. With respect to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ it has a matrix $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}=[T]_{\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$, and with respect to $\mathcal{C}$ another matrix $[T]_{\mathcal{C}}$.
Let $P=P_{\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathcal{C}}$ (the matrix whose columns are the new basis vectors $\mathcal{C}$ written in the old coordinates $\mathcal{B}$). Then
[T]_{\mathcal{C}}=P^{-1}[T]_{\mathcal{B}}\,P.

Compose the three conversions: $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates $\xrightarrow{P}$ $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates $\xrightarrow{[T]_{\mathcal{B}}}$ $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates of the image $\xrightarrow{P^{-1}}$ $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates. By Theorem 9.14 the matrix of the composite is $P^{-1}[T]_{\mathcal{B}}P$, and it equals $[T]_{\mathcal{C}}$ since both send $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}$ to $[T\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}$.
Square matrices $A,B$ are similar, written $A\sim B$, if $B=P^{-1}AP$ for some invertible $P$.

Similarity is an equivalence relation ($A=I^{-1}AI$; $B=P^{-1}AP\Rightarrow A=(P^{-1})^{-1}BP^{-1}$; transitivity by multiplying). Theorem 10.4 says: similar matrices are exactly the matrices of one operator in different bases. Conversely, if $B=P^{-1}AP$ then the columns of $P$ form a basis in which the operator $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ has matrix $B$.

Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$, the matrix of a map in the standard basis. It sends $(1,1)\mapsto(4,4)=4(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)\mapsto(2,-2)=2(1,-1)$. In the basis $\mathcal{B}=((1,1),(1,-1))$, with $P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, the matrix becomes
P^{-1}AP=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
In the right basis the map is a pure stretch: by $4$ along $\mathbf{b}_1$ and by $2$ along $\mathbf{b}_2$. This is diagonalisation, the subject of Chapters 13–15.

The matrix of a map describes what the map does as seen through a particular set of coordinate axes. Choosing axes well can turn a complicated-looking matrix into a transparent one. Finding such a basis is the search for eigenvectors.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Reflection across a line, computed by change of basis

blocks.x: Let $L$ be the line through the origin with direction $\mathbf{u}=(1,2)/\sqrt5$ and $\mathbf{u}^\perp=(-2,1)/\sqrt5$. Reflection across $L$ fixes $\mathbf{u}$ and negates $\mathbf{u}^\perp$, so in the basis $(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{u}^\perp)$ its matrix is $D=\diag(1,-1)$. With $P=[\mathbf{u}\ \mathbf{u}^\perp]=\frac1{\sqrt5}\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, which satisfies $P^{-1}=P\T$,
[\text{refl}]_{\mathcal{S}}=PDP^{-1}=\tfrac15\begin{pmatrix}-3&4\\4&3\end{pmatrix}.
No trigonometry is needed: work in the basis where the map is easy and convert back.
A property of matrices that depends only on the underlying operator, not on the basis, must be unchanged under similarity.
If $B=P^{-1}AP$ then
$\det B=\det A$;
$\tr B=\tr A$;
$\rank B=\rank A$;
$B-\lambda I=P^{-1}(A-\lambda I)P$, so $A$ and $B$ have the same characteristic polynomial and the same eigenvalues (Chapter 13);
$B^k=P^{-1}A^kP$ for every integer $k\ge0$, and $B$ is invertible iff $A$ is.

(i) is Corollary 5.12. (iii) is Proposition 8.12(iii). For (ii) we need the identity $\tr(XY)=\tr(YX)$, proved below; then $\tr(P^{-1}AP)=\tr(APP^{-1})=\tr A$. (iv): $P^{-1}(A-\lambda I)P=P^{-1}AP-\lambda I$. (v): $(P^{-1}AP)^k=P^{-1}A^kP$ because the inner factors $PP^{-1}$ cancel.
$\tr(XY)=\tr(YX)$ whenever both products are defined, even if $X,Y$ are not square. The trace is linear, $\tr(A\T)=\tr A$, and $\tr(ABC)=\tr(BCA)=\tr(CAB)$ (cyclic, but not arbitrary, permutations).
$\tr(XY)=\sum_i\sum_jx_{ij}y_{ji}=\sum_j\sum_iy_{ji}x_{ij}=\tr(YX)$.

Two matrices can share rank, determinant, trace and even characteristic polynomial without being similar: $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ both have characteristic polynomial $(\lambda-1)^2$, but the first is $I$ (similar only to itself, since $P^{-1}IP=I$) while the second is not. The complete classification of matrices up to similarity is the Jordan form (Chapter 14).

A change of basis acts on the matrix of an operator by $A\mapsto P^{-1}AP$ (similarity). But if the matrix represents a bilinear form or quadratic form $\mathbf{x}\T A\mathbf{x}$, the change of variables $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ gives $A\mapsto P\T AP$ instead (congruence). These agree only when $P$ is orthogonal ($P^{-1}=P\T$), which is why orthogonal changes of basis are so convenient; they are the subject of Chapters 11 and 15–16.

Suppose we need $A^{100}$ and we have a basis $\mathbf{p}_1,\dots,\mathbf{p}_n$ in which $A$ is diagonal: $A=PDP^{-1}$ with $D=\diag(d_1,\dots,d_n)$. Then $A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$ with $D^k=\diag(d_1^k,\dots,d_n^k)$, which is trivial to evaluate.
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ from Example 10.6,
A^k=P\begin{pmatrix}4^k&0\\0&2^k\end{pmatrix}P^{-1}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}4^k+2^k&4^k-2^k\\4^k-2^k&4^k+2^k\end{pmatrix}.
Check $k=1$: $\frac12\begin{pmatrix}6&2\\2&6\end{pmatrix}=A$.

blocks.name: Interview check
blocks.title: why do we care about diagonalisation?

blocks.x: Diagonal matrices are the only ones you can raise to powers, exponentiate, invert and solve with by inspection. Any question about repeated application of a linear map ($A^k$, Markov chain long-run behaviour, Fibonacci-type recursions, $e^{At}$ for differential equations, stability of iterations) reduces to understanding $A$ in an eigenbasis. Change of basis is the technique that makes this possible.

The same vector has different coordinates in different bases: $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}=P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}$, with columns of $P$ being old basis vectors in new coordinates.
The same operator has different matrices: $[T]_{\mathcal{C}}=P^{-1}[T]_{\mathcal{B}}P$; these are similar matrices.
Rank, determinant, trace, characteristic polynomial and eigenvalues are similarity invariants; $\tr(XY)=\tr(YX)$.
A basis in which $T$ is diagonal makes powers and functions of $T$ easy; finding it is the eigenvector problem.
Quadratic forms change by congruence $P\T AP$, not similarity, unless $P$ is orthogonal.
Let $\mathcal{B}=((1,2),(3,5))$. Find $P_{\mathcal{S}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$, $P_{\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathcal{S}}$, and the $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates of $(4,7)$.
In $\mathcal{P}_2$ let $\mathcal{B}=(1,t,t^2)$ and $\mathcal{C}=(1,1+t,1+t+t^2)$. Find $P_{\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathcal{C}}$ and the $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates of $2+3t+t^2$.
The operator $T$ on $\R^2$ has standard matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$. Find its matrix in the basis $((1,0),(1,1))$ and show that it is diagonal.
Prove that similar matrices have the same trace and determinant, and give a $2\times2$ pair of non-similar matrices with equal trace and determinant.
Show that $\tr(XY)=\tr(YX)$ implies that no matrices satisfy $XY-YX=I$ in finite dimensions.
Compute $A^{10}$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ by finding a basis of eigenvectors; recognise the entries as Fibonacci numbers. (The eigenvalues are $\tfrac{1\pm\sqrt5}2$.)
The reflection across the line $y=x$ has standard matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Find its matrix in the basis $((1,1),(1,-1))$.
Let $A$ be a $2\times2$ matrix with $A^2=A$. Show that $A$ is similar to a diagonal matrix with entries $0$ or $1$. (Hint: Chapter 9, Exercise 9.7.)
